card.name: Alamikkali
card.tagline: A sacred commemorative dance uniting Hindu and Muslim heritage through charcoal ritual.
card.profile: Alamikkali is a sacred folk dance and festival performed in Kasargod, Kerala, and parts of Mangalore, Karnataka. Rooted in the commemoration of Muharram and the historical battle of Karbala, the ritual features Hindu performers taking on the role of Alami under the leadership of Muslim Sahibs (Hanafi fakir leaders). Participants paint their bodies in black charcoal with white spots, wear plant-fibre beards, and dance house-to-house before a final flame ceremony. The tradition embodies deep communal harmony, combining memorial narrative with energetic folk movement.
card.insight: In Kasargod, Hindu practitioners paint their bodies in charcoal and white spots to commemorate the historical battle of Karbala.

card.profile_long:
Alamikkali is a sacred ritualistic folk dance performed predominantly around Alamippalli near Kanhangad in Kasargod district, Kerala, as well as in neighboring Mangalore, Karnataka. The festival serves as a historical memorial to the Battle of Karbala and the martyrdom of Hazrat Imam Hussain, celebrated in alignment with Muharram. Organised historically by Hindustani-speaking Hanafi Muslims known as Sahibs or Tuluker—who originally arrived in the area during Tippu's military campaigns—the actual dancing roles are undertaken by members of the Hindu community, reflecting a deep tradition of cross-religious unity.

During the performance, Hindu dancers portray the Alami. Their appearance memorializes the dark attire and hardships of the historical battlefield. Dancers coat their entire bodies in black charcoal dotted with white spots, wear knee-length dhotis, and adorn themselves with caps made of areca spathe filled with Ixora coccinea flowers. They wear moustaches and beards fashioned from the fibrous leaves of the munda plant, alongside neck chains made of flowers and foliage. Walking strictly barefoot, groups of five to six Alami travel from house to house in villages to collect alms.

The dance movement is energetic and expressive rather than strictly codified. Dancers advance with loud, boisterous energy, striking sticks together and sounding attached bells. Upon arriving at a household, they set down their collection wallets and deep-bottomed vessels and dance vigorously in front of the home without strict adherence to formal rhythmic patterns. Movement is accompanied by vocal chanting characterized by distinct tonal verses, always beginning and ending with the refrain 'lassolayma... lasso... layma... layma... laymalo...'.

The festival culminates at Alamippalli, a primary venue distinguished by a rock-lined open floor shaped like a flame rather than a traditional mosque structure. The final ceremonies honor the fallen soldiers through dramatic rites, including the burning of a central flame in which participants roll, and the symbolic display of Vellikkaram, representing the memory of Imam Hussain.

sections.origins_and_history: Alamikkali originated as a folk commemoration of the Battle of Karbala during Muharram. The festival was historically organized and led by Hindustani-speaking Hanafi Muslim families known as Sahibs or Tuluker, who settled around Puthiyakota and regional forts during Tippu's campaign. Over time, the tradition evolved into a unique cross-religious observance where the role of the Alami is performed by members of the Hindu faith. The primary historical center is Alamippalli in Kasargod, with additional observances documented in Chithari and Kottikulam.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers move in small itinerant groups of five to six members, visiting homes across villages. They process barefoot with inflated energy, creating noise using hand-held sticks and attached bells. Before each residence, they lay down their alms collection vessels and execute an energetic, unstructured dance in front of the house without giving strict priority to rhythmic precision. The performance incorporates dynamic vocal chants and unstructured conversations framed entirely as song.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is predominantly vocal and percussion-driven by the participants themselves. Dancers carry sticks and bells which they strike and shake during their procession and dance to produce rhythmic sound. The songs feature a unique tone and verse structure, uniformly opening and closing with the specific phrase 'lassolayma... lasso... layma... layma... laymalo...'. Conversations between performers and householders are also rendered musically.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers apply black charcoal all over their bodies, decorated with white spots. They wear dhotis drawn up to the knees, caps made of spathe containing Ixora coccinea flowers, and chains of flowers and leaves around their necks. False beards and moustaches are constructed from munda plant fibers. Performers never wear shoes and carry a wallet alongside a deep-bottomed vessel for alms. The main setting is Alamippalli in Kasargod, which features a rock-lined floor shaped like a flame, alongside village residential yards.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The festival is observed during Muharram to commemorate the Battle of Karbala and honor Hazrat Imam Hussain and his fallen soldiers. The black body coating recalls the dark clothing of opposing armies, while the final ceremony involves lighting a fire and rolling in the flames to respect slain combatants. The rite of Vellikkaram symbolizes the memory of Imam Hussain's burial. The entire festival stands as a symbol of Hindu-Muslim unity.
sections.notable_figures: Rasool Sahib is documented as a notable historical fakir sahib from Echikkanam who organized and conducted the last traditional Alamikkali ceremonies.
sections.regional_variants: Celebrations are centered at Alamippalli in Kasargod district, with regional observances also conducted in Chithari, Kottikulam, and parts of Mangalore in Karnataka state.
sections.lineage: The tradition is handed down through Hanafi Muslim fakir families (such as the Echikkanam family line of Rasool Sahib) who lead the organization, while the performance roles are inherited and maintained by Hindu villagers.
